lead: ARM assembly and C call each other because both obey one rule: the AAPCS calling convention. The caller puts arguments in registers and the callee returns a value in R0. Assembly handles startup code, tight loops and hardware access; C handles most application logic. Only a few universities teach this mix at this depth.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.4, Chapter 6.5, Unit 3 assembly (stack and subroutines), and Unit 4 embedded C.

blocks.text: AAPCS means ARM Architecture Procedure Call Standard. It is the rule book for calls between C and assembly. R0-R3 carry the first four arguments; more arguments go on the stack. R0 also carries the return value. R4-R11 are callee-saved: a function that changes them restores them before it returns. R12, R13 (SP), R14 (LR) and R15 (PC) have special roles. SP must be 8-byte aligned at every public interface, because 64-bit values may be passed.

At a call the caller sets the arguments, then BL writes the return address into LR. A routine that itself calls another function must save LR first. The usual frame is PUSH {R4, LR} at entry and POP {R4, PC} at exit: it saves the callee-saved register and LR, and returns through PC. Small inline assembly such as __asm("NOP"); is allowed for hardware operations.

sections.h3: File layout and the SUM loop

blocks.text: Assembly files use directives. AREA names a code section, ENTRY marks the first instruction, EXPORT makes a symbol visible to the linker, and DCD stores a 32-bit constant such as N DCD 10. Labels are addresses. The label SUM is the function that C will call.

blocks.code:
AREA    SUMCODE, CODE, READONLY
        EXPORT  SUM
        ENTRY
SUM     PUSH    {R4, LR}      ; save R4 and return address
        MOV     R4, R1        ; R4 = N
        MOV     R0, #0        ; R0 = sum = 0
        CMP     R4, #0
        BLE     sum_done
sum_loop
        ADD     R0, R0, R4    ; sum = sum + N
        SUBS    R4, R4, #1    ; N = N - 1, set flags
        BNE     sum_loop
sum_done
        POP     {R4, PC}      ; restore R4 and return
        END
blocks.output: N = 10 in R1 -> on return R0 = 55 (0x37)

blocks.text: R1 carries N and R0 returns the sum. SUBS subtracts and sets flags; BNE loops while the result is not zero. For N=10 the additions are 10+9+...+1, so R0 becomes 55. R4 is callee-saved, so it is pushed and popped. LR is saved so the routine can return through POP {R4, PC}: the saved LR goes into PC. The two-register pair also keeps SP 8-byte aligned.

sections.h3: C and assembly calling each other

blocks.text: From C, declare the assembly function with a prototype: extern int SUM(int n); then call int s = SUM(10);. A one-argument C call puts 10 in R0. The SUM code above expects N in R1, so use a wrapper MOV R1, R0; B SUM, or declare a two-argument function and pass N as the second argument.

From assembly, put arguments in R0-R3 and use BL to call C. Save LR before the call, because BL overwrites it. R4-R11 are preserved by the C function, so a live value in R5 survives the call. Save R4-R11 at entry to your own routine only if your routine changes them, and restore them before you return. The caller must not assume R0-R3 survive a call.

figure.caption: The sum loop used by SUM: R0 is cleared, R4 counts down from N, and each pass adds R4 into R0. For N=10 the final R0 is 55.

spec.title: Sum loop subroutine
spec.aria: Flowchart for a sum loop: copy N into R4, clear R0, return zero if N is not positive, otherwise add R4 into R0, decrement R4, and repeat until R4 is zero.

examples.question: Write an ARM assembly subroutine SUM that returns 1+2+...+N in R0, with N passed in R1. Use a loop. Call it from C with N=10. State the final R0 and one register the subroutine must preserve if it uses it.
steps: Clear R0 = 0: this is the running sum.
Copy the count: R4 = R1. If R4 <= 0, branch straight to return with R0 = 0.
Loop body: R0 = R0 + R4, then R4 = R4 - 1.
Use SUBS and BNE to repeat while R4 is not zero.
R4 is callee-saved, so PUSH {R4, LR} at entry and POP {R4, PC} at exit protect it, and R1 is left unchanged.
examples.answer: Final R0 = 55 (0x37). R4 is restored by the push and pop; any other R4-R11 register the routine uses must also be saved.
examples.check:
n = 10
total = 0
for k in range(n, 0, -1):
    total += k
print(total)

traps: R0-R3 are not preserved across a call. Keep live values in R4-R11 or on the stack.
Assembly that uses R4-R11 must save and restore them; the C caller assumes they survive.
SP must be 8-byte aligned at public interfaces. PUSH {R4, LR} pushes 8 bytes; PUSH {R4} alone breaks alignment.
A one-argument C call puts the argument in R0, not R1. The SUM example expects R1, so use a wrapper or a second argument.
BL overwrites LR. A routine that calls another function must save LR first.

quiz.q: Which registers carry arguments 1 to 4 in AAPCS?
Why must a subroutine save LR before it calls another function?
quiz.a: BL overwrites LR with the new return address; the old return address, the subroutine's own way back, would be lost.

quiz.q: N=6 in R1. Trace SUM. Final R0?
C calls SUM(10) with extern int SUM(int n). Which register holds 10, and what must assembly do if SUM expects R1?
quiz.a: R0 holds 10; move R0 to R1 with a wrapper, or change the prototype to pass N as the second argument.

quiz.q: Why is PUSH {R4, LR} better than PUSH {R4} before a call?
quiz.a: It saves LR, which BL will overwrite, and pushes 8 bytes, keeping SP 8-byte aligned.

quiz.q: An assembly routine uses R5 and calls a C function. What must it save, and where?
quiz.a: At entry push R5 and LR, as PUSH {R5, LR}. LR must be saved because BL overwrites it; R5 because this routine uses a callee-saved register and must restore it for its own caller. Pop them back with POP {R5, PC} before returning.

quiz.q: What does EXPORT do in an assembly file?
quiz.a: Makes a symbol visible to the linker so C can call it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production firmware still uses this mix: startup code in assembly, drivers in C with small inline assembly, linker scripts placing vectors and stacks. Cortex-M follows the same AAPCS, but exception entry puts EXC_RETURN in LR, so stack alignment matters more.
